chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Mu'awiya ibn Hakim from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from al-Husayn ibn Ali al-Sayrafī from some of our companions, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about the Sa'i (walking) between al-Safa and al-Marwah, whether it is a mandatory obligation or a prophetic tradition, so he said, 'It is a mandatory obligation.'
I said, 'Is it not that Allah, Exalted and Mighty, said, "So there is no blame upon him who tawafs by them"?'

He said, 'That is in the Umrah of Qada (compensation). Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) commanded them to remove the idols from Safa and al-Marwah, but a man was occupied until the days passed, so the idols were put back. They came to him and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, so-and-so did not perform Sa'i between Safa and al-Marwah, and the idols have been put back.' So Allah, Exalted and Mighty, revealed, "So there is no blame upon him who tawafs by them," meaning, 'And upon them are the idols.'

And whoever leaves the Sa'i intentionally, his Hajj is invalidated and he must perform Hajj next year. And if he leaves it forgetfully, he must repeat the Sa'i, nothing more, and there is no penalty upon him. He narrated that.

key_terms.السَّعْيُ: Sa'i: The ritual walking between Safa and Marwah during Hajj and Umrah
key_terms.سُنَّةٌ: Sunnah: A prophetic tradition or recommended practice
key_terms.عُمْرَةُ الْقَضَاءِ: Umrat al-Qada: The compensatory Umrah performed to complete an incomplete or invalid Hajj

ai.seo_question: Is the Sa'i between Safa and Marwah a mandatory obligation or a sunnah in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes Sa'i as a fundamental pillar (fard) of Hajj, resolving the apparent contradiction in the Quranic phrase 'no blame upon him' by contextualizing it within the Umrah of Qada, where lingering idols necessitated a specific dispensation. This hadith, recorded in al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, underscores the jurisprudential distinction between intentional omission, which voids the Hajj, and forgetful omission, which requires only re-performance, reflecting the Shia emphasis on the continuity of ritual purity and completeness in pilgrimage rites.
